title: Charles Martinez
summary: Charles Martinez was a Chiricahua Apache Hampton Institute graduate, animal-husbandry worker, golf-club foreman, mechanic, and member of the Martinez family craft economy at Shinnecock.
content:
Charles Martinez was a Chiricahua Apache Hampton Institute graduate whose documented life connected animal husbandry, work on the Shinnecock Reservation, long service at the National Golf Club, mechanical skill, and the Martinez family's Native craft economy. The selected sources do not establish his birth date, death date, exact marriage date, or precise employment years, so this biography keeps those limits visible.1

Hampton Institute and Shinnecock

Stone identifies Charles as Chiricahua Apache and a Hampton Institute graduate. David Bunn Martine's 1995 family account adds that his grandfather studied animal husbandry at Hampton, came to work on a farm on the Shinnecock Reservation, and married the farmer's daughter, Alice Bunn. Together, these accounts document Charles's arrival and family connection without supplying a date for the move or marriage.2

Golf-club and mechanical work

Stone says Charles worked for twenty-three years as a foreman at the National Golf Club. Another section shows Alice's husband operating an early tractor at the golf club and describes him as an expert mechanic and owner of automobiles that later became classics. He also operated a gasoline station on the west side of West Gate Road and Montauk Highway. Because the source does not provide exact years for these activities, the related Historic Moment is labeled as an early-twentieth-century record rather than assigned an invented date.3

The Martinez family trading post

Stone credits Alice with opening the first Indian trading post on Long Island in 1939 and establishing the permanent post after returning from Oklahoma in 1953. The same account says the Martinez family made the beadwork, handicraft, and wood carving sold there. This record situates Charles within a family enterprise while keeping the founding role with Alice, as the source states.4

A circa-1934 community record

A circa-1934 photograph caption names Charles and Alice Bunn Martinez at Conscience Point among other Shinnecock community participants. The caption establishes the names, place, and approximate date only. It does not identify a pageant, performance, regalia, ages, household roles, or motives.5

What the sources do not establish

A later family-history article identifies Chin-Chee as David Bunn Martine's great-grandfather, but the available passage does not resolve the intermediate generation clearly enough to define Charles's exact relationship to Chin-Chee. This profile therefore does not publish a specific Chin-Chee lineage.

Reading the map

The map uses broad public locations associated with Charles's documented work and the existing Conscience Point record. The line is a source guide, not a reconstruction of his private or exact travel route.

References

  • Gaynell Stone, ed., The Shinnecock Indians: A Culture History, vol. VI (1983), pp. 12, 329, and 351.
  • David Bunn Martine, “Shinnecock's Own Historian,” Southampton Star (1995).
  • National Golf Links of America, official location record, Sebonac Inlet Road, Southampton.
why_this_matters: Charles Martinez's surviving record connects off-reservation education with work, family, and Native enterprise at Shinnecock. Keeping the gaps in his dates and lineage visible makes the biography more useful: it presents what the sources establish without turning family memory into an unsupported genealogy.
activity_update_summary: Added a date-cautious biography of Chiricahua Apache Hampton Institute graduate, golf-club foreman, mechanic, and Shinnecock community family member Charles Martinez.
